utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Alex Demirdjian, Catherine Loftus, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for the Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And I note this morning for the record that we reconvene under Rule 15 bis; Judge Harhoff being absent. We have been alerted that counsel on both sides would wish to raise something arising out of the last issue which was canvassed yesterday. But before we hear from counsel, there's a comment that I would wish to make and which may assist counsel in anything further that they have to say, and it is this. And I recognise that in response to the query -- to the issue that was raised by Ms. Korner from the Office of the Prosecution that the response that I would have, given that she would have had rather short shrift, and I plead in my own defence the pressure of time because we were very near the adjournment, what I would wish to add is this: Without gainsaying the overriding or overarching principle of relevance which governs all trials, and relevance being determined by the pleadings, which in the case of a criminal matter is the indictment, in reality it is recognised that the indictment is -- being related to certain historical events is necessarily selective, indeed some even may say in some cases arbitrary, in order for a trial to be made manageable. But the near artificiality almost of drawing a line around what the indictment lays out in terms of charges means that very often, and this is not the first time it is has arisen, it arose from time to time during the case for the Prosecution, that in order to make sense, and this is especially so in proceedings such as that in which we are engaged in terms what would have happened in the former Yugoslavia during the time-period that is set out in the Statute, there is -- it is often necessary for -- in order to set a context, both temporally and geographically, for a witness to be led beyond the strict confines of the indictment, the challenge always is. And in this context, the Chamber must rely on the experience and good sense and goodwill of counsel leading it to guide the witness in such a way that such -- that any such necessary contextual or ancillary matters do not stray too far outside the confines of -- and I come back to the broad term of relevance. And if I may use the example of what would have happened over the past two or three days, it may not be apparent when counsel takes a particular line as to whether, even in terms of the question or document which is sought to be admitted, it is, on the face of it, relevant, and the Chamber inquires, and depending on counsel's response, the Chamber may or may not be satisfied and rule accordingly. So to return specifically to the question that was posed by Ms. Korner, I think the more nuanced answer to which she would be entitled, and this having been raised on the record, this explanation is added in this context, is that to the extent that it becomes apparent that evidence may have been permitted to be led by the side calling the witness, may arguably appear to be somewhat outside of the confines, that logically the side opposite would be permitted and must be properly permitted to explore those areas. And I trust that the explanation that I have sought to give this morning hasn't further muddled the matter and that counsel is more assisted than they would have been by what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm very grateful for that clarification. Indeed, although it not the real matter that I want to deal with this morning, I was going to return to that matter for clarification. And if I may, at the end of what I have to say about the matter that Mr. Zecevic raised yesterday, I will return to that. But, Your Honour, what I want to deal with this morning is what Mr. Zecevic raised at the beginning of yesterday's proceedings, when he applied for a sanction against the Prosecution for what I understood to be a violation of our obligations under Rule 68, because he applied for a sanction under Rule 68 bis, but which has been clarified by e-mail this morning or, rather, I'm sorry, last night, that we're in violation of our obligations under Rule 66(B). I also understood, which must be right, because some of the documents that were mentioned yesterday as not disclosed before, do not come within the category of Rule 66(B), that there is also an application that all documents that we propose to use in cross-examination as notified when the witness goes into the witness box, must have been disclosed in advance. And it's those two aspects that I need to deal with this morning. Your Honours, Mr. Zecevic rattled off a series of cases which we took the opportunity to look at, and, Your Honours, it seems to me that I should start with the position of the law in this Tribunal as it appears to be. And with the greatest of respect, I don't think that any of the authorities that Mr. Zecevic quoted yesterday really assist the Court at all on this aspect. Your Honours, he began with the Lukic and Lukic decision on the 3rd of November, 2008. Your Honours, in summary, that authority deals with the situation where it was said by the Defence that material relating to a Prosecution witness had not been disclosed, as it ought to have been. So, Your Honours, I do not see how that is at all relevant to the issue that Your Honours have to consider now. The second matter was Rule 68, and it doesn't appear that this is the argument, in relation to Karadzic. Now it doesn't need repeating because everybody knows there has been a series of disclosure problems in the Karadzic case which has resulted in various adjournments, but, again, the complaint that was made in that case is a failure to provide Rule 68 material in respect of Prosecution witnesses. The Bralo case seems even more removed, it would seem to us, from what we're dealing with here, because this was an application on appeal, Mr. Bralo having pleaded guilty to various offences. And I can quote from page 10 of the Judgement of the 30th of August, 2006: "The Appellant seeks an order from the Appeals Chamber directing the Prosecution to comply with its obligations under Rule 66 and Rule 68 of the Rules and, in particular, to identify material obtained from the Appellant which the Prosecutor has used or intends to use in any other proceedings as well as the cases in which such use occurred or is intended to occur and the reasons for such use or reference; and (b) to declare that the Prosecution is unaware of any other material capable of being relevant to sentence." And, Your Honour, the second -- the next paragraph, 22, says: "The Appellant particularly focuses on his motion for disclosure on two categories of documents relevant to his cooperation with the Prosecution; those provided by the Appellant in 1997 that he claims were used in at least two other cases before the Tribunal, and documents of 2005 which may be used in the Blaskic review proceedings." And finally, Your Honour, Karemera, which is the Rwanda case, 2006, was whether the Prosecution's Rule 68 obligations could be subsumed by the use of EDS, to which the answer was no and we entirely accept that. And we have never sought to argue that our Rule 68 obligations are satisfied by the fact that the document is on EDS. If there's a Rule 68 document, we have an obligation to disclose it personally to the Defence. But as I say, Your Honour, it doesn't seem to me that any of these cases have any application whatsoever to the problem that now faces Your Honour; namely, the complaint, as I say, which is a two-fold one, one, that we haven't complied with our obligations under Rule 66(B), and can I say straight away that Mr. Zecevic is right in that on some of these documents, and I'll explain in a moment what -- why that is. But the second matter is whether we have an obligation to disclose material which is -- we're going to use in cross-examination which has not hitherto been disclosed and doesn't come under the provisions of the Rule 68 or 66(B). Your Honours, we would say that the authorities which are the most relevant on this begin with the case of Boskoski on the 31st of January, 2008, where the Defence -- there was Defence motion that requested that the Chamber order the Prosecutor to disclose any statement, audio-video, or any other record, decision or note that mentions any of the Boskoski Defence witnesses; any statement, audio video, or other record, decision or note sought and obtained by the Prosecutor in relation to a particular witness; any statements or notes taken after the filing of the Boskoski Defence of its witness list that make reference to the role, function or proposed evidence of any of the proposed witnesses. Effectively that's this. The Prosecution responded that it would not disclose material that pertains to the credibility of Defence witnesses, referring to the Rules and practice of this trial, which, in its view, permit a party to withhold material going to credibility until the start of cross-examination. And that's what we have been effectively relying on. Your Honour, the decision cites the case of Bagosora, that's B-a-g-o-s-o-r-a, and may I say I gave this list to the Defence last night, Your Honours, and made sure that they were aware of it, of the 25th of September, 2006. And this is actually referred to in the -- the Boskoski Judgement at paragraph 10: "The Appeals Chamber observes that this plain reading of Rule 66(B) of the Rules does not create a broad, affirmative obligation on the Prosecution to disclose any and all documents which may be relevant to its cross-examination, as suggested by the Defence." Your Honour, the ruling in the Boskoski case, -- and can I say there have been a number of different rulings in various Trial Chambers here, but this is perhaps the fullest. The -- at paragraph 8, the Appeals Chamber has held that this rule, 66(B), applies to material which is relevant to the selection of witnesses for the Defence case, as this is an important element of the preparation of the Defence. Documents or other records relevant to credit therefore may, in certain circumstances, may be considered material for the purposes of Rule 66(B). An example of this is where a document relevant to credit may be capable of influencing a decision whether to call a certain witness or not. And I suppose one could give an example, though no examples are given here. The Prosecution were in possession of a statement by a proposed Prosecution witness where, in effect, he confessed that he'd taken part in some killings or beatings or something of that nature. Well, clearly that might affect the decision to call. Your Honours, there's further consideration of this particular issue in the Popovic case, on the 4th of November, 2008. And then, finally -- and the 17th of December of 2008, and finally, in the Prlic case on the 26th of February, 2009, and -- which is the Appeals Chamber one, I think ... yes. The Appeals Chamber decision there, dealing with the 13th of January, 2009, decision by the Prlic Trial Chamber. It's not quite on point because the issue was the question of brand new documents but, nonetheless, it deals with this particular aspect of the obligation to disclose under Rule 66(B) and whether -- it really -- as I say, it's more about whether they can be admitted as exhibits if they're only produced during the course of cross-examination. So we -- effectively we say that the two major cases on this are the Bagosora decision which was an Appeals Chamber decision, I should say, although it is quite old. Your Honours, if there is any other point in the law that Mr. Zecevic wishes to raise, I'm sure he will. Now can I move to the actual complaint in this case. Your Honours, Mr. Zecevic listed out and finally checked that we had a revised list of documents on our list which had not been disclosed and which he suggests comes under Rule 66(B). Now, Your Honours -- and I'll wait to be corrected if I'm wrong because I would never guarantee that our correspondence with the Defence is entirely accurate. We certainly, many, many years ago, before Mr. Krgovic came into the case, received a Rule 66(B) request from counsel then acting on behalf of Zupljanin but limited to certain matters. We then from Stanisic, who had not invoked the rule -- although interestingly enough, as I pointed out, we had actually been, as it were, voluntarily making disclosures of certain matters. On the 15th of October, 2009, we received a letter from Mr. Zecevic or on behalf -- sorry, from both Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Cvijetic which effectively - and if necessary we can give Your Honour a copy - asked for everything and anything that had ever moved in this case. All information received from persons who have personal knowledge of all events in the indictment; all information from persons who have testified as Defence witnesses; all information received from the Bosnian government; all information received -- and so on and so forth. And, Your Honours, the response that we gave was this was a wholly unrealistic request that -- in fact, we described it as wide-ranging and imprecise and said that accordingly, unless you provide more realistic parameters for any searches to be done and more detail of why these matters are material to the preparation of your Defence, we are unable to comply with your request. Your Honour, we then had various short and much more specific requests for material which I -- if Mr. Zecevic wants to refer to them, that's fine. But I think that the real one in this case or for these documents is this. After the to-ing and fro-ing over then-Colonel now General Lisica's documents and his book and all the [indiscernible] and I accept entirely buried in our vaults Mr. Milosevic had, in fact, given us way back in 2004 a copy of the book but we weren't aware of it, as you would have gathered. The -- was a request dated the 21st of January, the Defence kindly requests urgent disclosure of all documents relating from TG3 Doboj; all documents originating from the city defence Doboj; all documents originating from the city defence Derventa; all documents signed by Colonel Slavko Lisica; all documents signed by Andrija Bjelosevic. Accordingly we instituted searches and I believe that certainly in relation to the -- we disclosed a very large number of documents including some 300 or so, I believe, that were actually documents signed by Mr. Bjelosevic. Over 200 I'm told, Your Honours. We can -- when we get searches - it is necessary to explain this - we give them search parameters and, indeed, we actually extended the search parameter not just signed but any documents provided to us by Mr. Bjelosevic, although that wasn't within the request. When you get the searches back, and we have actually printed out what happens if anybody wants to see them, they come in various different sections. One of the sections is documents not authored by, not received from. Therefore, they may affect Mr. Bjelosevic but neither authored by -- so we didn't check that section. And as it turns out, Your Honour, some of the documents that are on the Defence list, and we can show them to the Defence or to Your Honours if you want, turned up, and we don't know why, in that section. But, the whole matter is -- is rather odd, as I will now go on to explain. Your Honours, it may be as well if we have up on the screen, if we can, the -- our document list. In Sanction. The list of documents that we sent. Thank you. Your Honours, the Defence say, and we accept that these documents were not disclosed in advance, that the first document number 2 is -- was not disclosed in advance. We accept that. We say we had no obligation to disclose it. It does not come under Rule 68 or Rule 66(B). Your Honours, we -- we rely on that. We are not obliged to disclose in advance the documents that are only pertinent to cross-examination. Well, and when I say "in advance," I mean obviously we have to disclose once the witness goes into the witness box. And, Your Honour, may I say, there would be no point in having the ruling that we don't have to disclose until such time what documents we're going to use in cross-examination if, in fact, we had to reveal all the documents well in advance. The obvious effect is which gives the witness and the Defence a chance to tailor their evidence which is not the point of cross-examination, particularly when you're testing credibility. Your Honours, number 3, same thing. We say no obligation to disclose. It's another intercept. Now, Your Honours, 5, I am afraid is one of the oddities. During the course of his conversation with the Office of the Prosecutor in -- in 2004, Mr. Bjelosevic handed over -- the interview went over, I think, two or three days. And on the second day he came back with his own personal notes of an incident. And they were handed over to the investigator. He signed them, I believe, as either AB 1 or AB 2. They're contained in the interview. And, Your Honour, I have no explanation at all for why, when we turned over the 2004 interview, we didn't hand over at the same time the documents that Mr. Bjelosevic had given to us. He gave us a large number. This particular -- and we handed over the 2004 interview on the 20th of July, 2009. And according to Mr. Zecevic on Monday, they're using that interview as the basis for his examination-in-chief. And I'm going to return to that because I have, in the light of what's being going on, severe doubts about that. But, therefore, they must have read it or listened to it. At no -- I mean, it's not an excuse, but it is odd is all I can say. Have we ever had a request for the documents that Mr. Bjelosevic handed over in the interview until that very late one which came in January of this year? So, Your Honour, I don't know why that was -- and I don't know why we didn't disclose them at the time. But it was there for them to see. And there's no specific reference to it. This -- it never was translated either. It seems to have disappeared into one of these black holes and they're being translated at present. As you will see, it says "Translation requested" on the screen. And it turned up under not authored by and not received from. We simply have no explanation for why that is. Your Honour, item number 6, again, was a document given to us by Mr. Bjelosevic in interview. I've forgotten what the AB marking is. Document number 7 is the same. And, again, it just seems to have disappeared because we didn't even ask for a translation. Oh, and indeed now, Your Honour, that's the other point. So -- there can be absolutely no prejudice to the Defence on this at all, but in fact, Mr. Smith has kindly reminded me, it has turned up in the Defence list of exhibits as 1D437. So clearly, they got their own copy from Mr. Bjelosevic, which doesn't surprise me. I imagine that everything Mr. Bjelosevic gave us he gave to the Defence and more, and I'm going to return to that again, Your Honour, at the end of what I have to say. The next document I understand that there's disclosure -- the complaint is -- is that at 16. Go to item number 16. Again, Your Honour, handed over by Mr. Bjelosevic in the interview. 23 is the next one, I believe. I should be corrected if I've got anything wrong. Your Honours, this one I think -- can I just check what that is. I'm reminded by Mr. Demirdjian helpfully. Your Honours, this is a Kezic document not authored by or received from Mr. Bjelosevic. We say we had no obligation to disclose this. 28 is the next one. This again is one that was handed over to Mr. Bjelosevic at interview. And is in fact on the Defence list as 65 ter 00194D1. 30, again, handed over in the interview, this time in 2009, marked by him as AB 3. 31, handed over in interview in 2004. Also on the Defence list as 65 ter 196D1. 33, again, handed over by Mr. Bjelosevic in the interview, marked by him AB 2. That was the 2009 interview. And again it came up, Your Honours, under the section not authored by or received from in the ISU searches. And I believe, Your Honour, that's the last of the documents. No, sorry, the one that's -- sorry. 86 on our list. Your Honour, that one we say that falls under no 66(B) request. The same with 87. The same with 88. And the last is number 90. This was a sketch made by Mr. Bjelosevic in the interview in 2004. 94 -- oh, sorry. Yes, sorry, 94 on our list was marked AB 10 in 2004 by Mr. Bjelosevic who handed it over, and again, it came up under the section of not authored by, not received. And 97, we say is not a document that falls under any 66(B) request. So, Your Honours, I accept we are in violation of the 66(B) request as regards the specific documents that, for some reason, as I say, should have been disclosed that related to the interviews with Mr. Bjelosevic. But as I say, certainly it's a lesson learned that we cannot check things that -- under the ISU searches that say not authored by or not received by. But we say it has nothing to do with any sanctions under Rule 68, and, in any event, there is no prejudice at all to the Defence. However, Your Honours, I return to the question of our obligation to disclose in advance documents which we intend to use in cross-examination and which do not fall under proper Rule 66(B) requests. It is our contention, based on the authorities here, and based on, in fact common sense, that we have no obligation to disclose until such time as the witness has gone into the witness box and we give our list of exhibits which we wish to use for cross-examination. So, Your Honours, those are our submissions on this matter that was raised by Mr. Zecevic yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I need some clarification. What about the document in your tab 34, what is your position in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wasn't aware that was one that was under -- one that hadn't been disclosed. It's not one -- wasn't on the list. Oh, was it? Oh, right. Right. Your Honour, and I'm so sorry, you're quite right. This one should have been disclosed not under, I suppose, any Rule 66(B) -- well, no, actually I think it probably -- because I'm pretty certain we would had a 66(B) from Mr. Zupljanin's counsel. I'm sorry, this just fell through the net. I don't know why we didn't disclose it because it's is clear it is addressed to Stojan Zupljanin and it should have been disclosed under all circumstances. I don't know how it fell through. So I accept entirely that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly your submission, you use this document relating to the credibility of Mr. Bjelosevic. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Particularly this document you will use because I'm interested only in that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document that we intend to ask Mr. Bjelosevic about because his name appears at the top. It's not authored by him or anything like that. But it's -- it goes to his relationship with Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will be very short, Your Honours, I'm trying to save the time. The authorities that we cited were related to the -- to the question of whether the EDS is -- is equal to the -- the disclosure obligation by the Office of the Prosecutor, because we anticipated that that is going to be the argument that the -- that the Office of the Prosecutor will use. That is -- that was the only purpose for the authorities that we cited. Your Honours, let me be very clear. Rule 68 bis is the only rule in the Rules of Procedure, and it covers all disclosure obligations. It doesn't cover only 68. It covers 66 as well. So that's the only Rule that covers the disclosure obligations. Failure to comply with the disclosure obligation. And it goes for all Rules that provide for the disclosure obligation. Your Honours, we, in our -- in my submission, I listed all the documents that were not disclosed to us by the Office of the Prosecutor, and we say they should have been disclosed to us on the -- on the basis of Rule 66(B). Now, some of them are on our list, that's true. And -- but it doesn't change the fact that these documents were in possession and they should have been disclosed to us by the Office of the Prosecutor. We received them during our preparation of the Defence case from the witness. And the last point, Your Honours, in our opinion, we say, Rule 66(B) overrides disclosure by the Office of the Prosecution when examination-in-chief begins. That is our position. So the Rule 66(B) must be applied and the Office of the Prosecutor is expected and it must disclose to us, based on Rule 66(B), documents which Ms. Korner correctly cited were, for some reason, lost or, I don't know, in a black hole or whatever the wording was used. However, I understand that this might happen, but, still, it doesn't change the fact that it is -- it is highly prejudicial to the Defence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, obviously -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... on that matter I have and I've dealt with. I say there is no prejudice, quite obviously, because they have got these documents, and that's something I want to come back to. Your Honours may recall that at the end of Monday's hearing, after Mr. Zecevic had finished opening the case, Judge Harhoff asked for statements made by Defence witnesses, and Mr. Zecevic told the Court, and this is at page 19404, that the 92 ter witnesses they were relying -- proposed 92 ter they were relying on [indiscernible] interviews that we had done with those witnesses, one of the witnesses gave an additional statement, he said, top of page 19405, part of the package also disclosed -- already disclosed to Your Honours. All other witnesses, none of them gave any statements although they were on -- the majority of them were on the list of the Office of the Prosecutor. Well, that is not actually quite right, but I'm not concerned with that. Mr. Hannis, who was in court, said this: "I have a concern and a question, I guess. The interviews that were given to the Prosecution that did not result in any statements being created were generally tape-recorded conversations, and you have seen or heard some of those transcripts of those. I guess I'm wondering out loud is the Defence saying that they took no statements from any of their witnesses. There are no witness statements other than, I think, the one that has been disclosed. If they have investigator notes or tape-recorded interviews of their witnesses and they're willing to disclose those to the Trial Chamber, then that would affect our position as to what we want to do. "Mr. Zecevic: We don't have any notes, nor recorded interviews. We relied on their interviews given to the Office of the Prosecutor and based on that we spoke to the witnesses." Your Honours, I may say, I express some reservations about that in the light of the tonnes of evidence that has been given over the last two days by Mr. Bjelosevic which isn't remotely dealt with in any of the interviews that were conducted with him. But, Your Honours, my point, I'm afraid, is a slightly different one. Your Honours may recall that Mr. Zecevic yesterday raised that we knew that Mr. Bjelosevic was a Defence witness, and we agreed that a number of the witnesses had told us that they were going to be Defence witnesses. I then went -- and I said I would check, because I wasn't entirely sure what Mr. Bjelosevic had told us, so I went back last night and checked in the 2009 interview. I believe it's in e-court, isn't it? I wonder if we could have it put up. All right. It may not matter, Your Honours. I can read it. At the end of the interview, and it starts at -- it's a separate -- unfortunately, the pagination here -- because each tape seems to have been typed separately, but it's the last tape. It's page 2 of 5 in T001-1858. All right, I'll read -- Your Honours, I'm sorry, it's not that easy to find. The investigator was confirming that -- with Mr. Bjelosevic that when he had been spoken to on the phone, he had said that he was likely to be the witness of Mr. Stanisic, yes. That you asked us to speak to his lawyer Mr. Zecevic, yes. And in the subsequent telephone conversation, I told you that I informed my STA, Joanna Korner, and she had done so accordingly. And I told you that the reply that we got from Mr. Zecevic was that the decision is purely yours if you want to talk to us. It is now in Sanction, Your Honours. It's coming up on the screen. Question by the investigator at the top of the next page, please. "I want to ask you whether you've made a statement to the investigators for Mr. Stanisic, the Defence investigators? "Yes, I have, to Slobodan. First name Slobodan. I forgot his last name. A lawyer from Bijeljina, anyway, from the team. I think that was about two years ago. We had short interviews and he made some notes relating to this interview. "We just need to confirm for the purposes of the tape that you, in fact, made a statement to them. We're not asking what you said to them. "This was -- this was the initial statement. We didn't have much contact later on, but Zecevic, lawyer Zecevic, confirmed to me they are counting on my" and that was inaudible. "And so from your point of view, you are still prepared to testify on behalf of Mr. Stanisic about the facts that I know." Your Honour, it is absolutely clear that there are notes of the conversations with Mr. Bjelosevic. I now make a formal request, which we haven't done so far, under 66(B), that all notes of conversations and all documents handed over by Mr. Bjelosevic to the Defence are provided -- copies are provided to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, again, there are no statements. There are no notes. We don't have investigators. We never took any statements from the witnesses except the ones disclosed. However, Ms. Korner knows that this case has been going on, the preparation in the pre-trial in this case, Mr. Stanisic's Defence case, the overall Stanisic case started in 2005, when I was only appointed in late 2008. So everything what happened before, Ms. Korner is well aware, very well aware, as well as the Trial Chamber, I believe, at least the Pre-Trial Judge, about the problems that I experienced asking for the documentation from the previous lead counsel Mr. Bezbradica. Where in fact I haven't received any. And the actual disclosure of the OTP has never been provided, and after I took over the case, I asked that the disclosure be repeated from the day one to me. Now concerning this situation that Ms. Korner has brought up, I guesses Mr. Cvijetic can explain this situation or maybe provide some information about it, because I can't. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Back at the time when lead counsel in this case was Mr. Bezbradica, we toured the field, as it were, where we were making a preliminary screening of potential Defence witnesses among individuals who had not been placed on the Prosecution list. These were just interviews in the sense that we wanted to hear from these individuals whether they had already decided that they would be Prosecution witnesses or whether they could be, in fact, Defence witnesses. In that process, we did not take any substantial information from them, especially not reports. We merely wanted to hear if they wanted to be Defence witnesses and gave them an outline of the possible issues that we might elicit evidence from them on that point. At that point we didn't know whether they would be Defence witnesses. We could not make that decision before we received the Prosecution 65 ter list. So that is where it for the most part ended, at the preliminary conversation, exchange of contact details and -- until such time as we would possibly contact them later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hear the Defence response. They have no notes. Mr. Cvijetic's notes don't exist, I take it, and no statement of any sort from this man, and they're calling him absolutely blind. Well, that's their position. But the second matter that I raise is that I would like now copies of all the documents that Mr. Bjelosevic turned over to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a second and let me consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Rule 66(B) does not apply to -- to the Defence. It applies only to the Office of the Prosecutor. However, I can assure Ms. Korner that, as far as I know, all documents that have been disclosed to -- to us by Mr. Bjelosevic which have any relevance are on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I made a mistake on the rule. Of course it's -- it's Rule 67. They apply under Rule 66. We apply under Rule 67. So I make the application under Rule 67. I'm not asking for documents whether they're relevant or not. I'm asking what the Defence consider to be relevant, which appears to be a far wider field than we would seem to be relevant because, as we've seen for the last two days, we've been covering huge areas unrelated to this indictment. I'm asking under Rule 67(A)(i), although I see I'm out of time. So I should have done this before, in fact. Your Honours, it shows one should always check the rules. Within the time limit prescribed by the Trial Chamber at a time -- no, I'm sorry. Yes, at a time not prior to ruling under Rule 90 but not less than one week prior to the commencement of the Defence case. But it seems I'm out of time, Your Honour, so I will have to approach it from a different angle. Your Honours, finally, can I return to the matter that arose yesterday and that Your Honours dealt with this morning. Your Honours, the first matter is this: None of what has been said by this man for the last two days, nearly five hours, not none, that's exaggeration, but as I put it yesterday, something like 10 to 15 per cent actually deals with the matters that are covered by this indictment, and what is more, nothing of this appears in the 65 ter summary. There is no indication that this witness was going to deal with the events in Brod, Slavonski or Bosanski, no indication that he was going to deal with the events in Derventa and so on and so forth. Your Honours, we would ask that for future witnesses we get proper 65 ter summaries so that we can object in advance. What's been happening here is, of course, we have had no notice of this, and though I've been making the objections throughout, it is much more difficult. And we accept that Mr. Zecevic is entitled to adduce through the witness the reasons which, as he put, why the split in the MUP took place, which is unrelated to any suggestion that there was -- this was part of the joint criminal enterprise to carve out the Serb state. The split in the MUP. That, of course, of course, he is entitled to lead such evidence as is relevant to that. But there must come a point where we stray into completely irrelevant evidence. And yesterday's long answer at the very end, unstopped, which wasn't an answer to Mr. Zecevic's question at all, Mr. Zecevic let this go on, which had absolutely nothing to do with the question that was asked and was the Serb view of the events that he was describing. So, Your Honour, we say there has to come a limit and it's for Your Honours, not really us, to say, This does not come within the terms of relevant matters to the indictment, nor indeed is it covered by the 65 summary. It is unfortunate that Prosecution counsel has to keep leaping to their feet the whole time and saying, This is not relevant. Your Honours, as regards what's gone on so far, we will have to cross-examine on some of the matters that he has raised because, as we say, our case is that it is a very partial, one-sided view of the events that he described and he has omitted a number of events that Your Honours may feel are relevant. Although we should say we accept entirely that that part of Bosnia and Croatia, there was continual conflict going on from very early stages all the way through 1992, but not in the way or not in the limited way that this witness has described. And I'm afraid that that extends the time that we will require for cross-examination. We based our estimates for cross-examination on the fact that the -- what was going to be led from the witness was specifically relevant to the matters on the indictment and specifically relevant to -- or covered by the 65 ter summary. And so, Your Honours, that is the actual situation we're in at the moment. As I say, we don't intend to spend anything like the time that Mr. Zecevic has spent with this witness on events outside the parameter of the indictment, but we will have to deal with some of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will briefly respond again. I don't think that making submissions at this point is appropriate. But, however, I will give my explanation. Your Honours, yesterday, page 19560, 24, my question was: "Could you explain to us what the situation was like in the territory of the Doboj CSB, what stations were you in contact with, the SJB stations in relation to which station the hierarchy functioned and the standard procedures of MUP? Could you please describe that to us." On page 19561, after I stopped the witness to give an explanation, he says, on line 23: "By your leave, Your Honours, I would like to elaborate on this event and on the actions of the members of MUP in Bosnia-Herzegovina in response to that ..." And then he goes into the territory which I agree is not relevant to specifics of the case. However, Your Honours, I have been cautioned at least six or seven times during the Prosecutor's case even by Your Honours when stopping the witness. That is why I was reluctant to stop him and that is why I didn't stop him. And, as a matter of fact, he was actually asking for permission by Your Honours to elaborate on that. Now, I -- I definitely and totally disagree with Ms. Korner just said. All this is very relevant. If Ms. Korner stands on the position that the CSB Doboj is not part of their allegations and the part of the indictment, then she should say so. Because it is my understanding that we have the MUP of RS and we have the CSBs on the next level. According to my reading of the indictment, some or all chiefs of the CSBs are alleged members of the joint criminal enterprise. Now, what I wanted to show is the relationship between the CSB Doboj and the MUP of Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in parallel to their relation to MUP of RS, Republika Srpska. It is not my -- there is nothing I can do that, at that point, the issue that they were discussing between the MUP of Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the CSB Doboj was the situation in -- in Bosanski Brod, in Derventa. This is the fact of the matter and the -- and the situation that happened over there. Therefore, in order to properly understand, this evidence must have been -- must have been heard in Court. That is all I need. I'm not going to use any more of your time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, in terms of the last two issues which have been canvassed by counsel, I don't think it's necessary for the Chamber to say anything further at this point. In terms of the first matter, and that harks back to the motion, I suppose it is, without notice that would have been made by Mr. Zecevic at the beginning of yesterday's hearing, it is obvious -- well, it should be obvious to counsel that the issues are such that the Chamber is not in a position to rule extemporaneously and would have to consider carefully the submissions made by counsel and the authorities cited in support. I notice that it is 10.05, which is about 20 minutes short of when we would ordinarily rise. I'm wondering if, whether -- and I'm thinking out loud. I'm wondering whether we should stagger the sitting today, and in that context, I should alert counsel that I'm going to have to -- we're going to have take the adjournment at 1.25 because I have a meeting with one of the other Judges, and the only convenient time for him is 1.30, which is before the ordinary time for rising today. So I'm wondering whether it would be -- the practical course would be to take the first break now and then have the witness in and adjust the remaining sittings accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We -- we do not oppose it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would resume in 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Would the Usher please escort the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may be seated. Good morning to you, Mr. Bjelosevic. As a matter of courtesy I should explain that the reason why you would have been kept waiting for an hour and a half is that, as is not unusual in trials, from time to time there are procedural matters with which the Court must deal, and virtually the whole of what would have been the first session this morning was taken up with those matters. So we are only now in a position to resume your evidence. And before I invite Mr. Zecevic to begin, I would remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, yesterday we adjourned at the end of a long day, I imagine for you as well. The last question had to do with the situation as it existed in the public security stations subordinated to you. My question had to do with what was the situation like in these SJBs in general at the end of -- at the end of April 1992 and in individual SJBs.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started explaining what the situation was like in SJBs, and I started my account from the north, heading towards the south. Can I ask Their Honours whether I should complete my explanation as to what the situation was really like at the time, or should I leave that story unfinished? Because if I speak briefly, I'm afraid that the picture I will paint will not be a complete one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I tried to focus you on the issues relevant to us. I do understand your need to paint the whole picture for us, but we have to stick to what is strictly relevant. So can you give us just a brief outline of the situation in each of the SJBs, what was their situation, what was your communication with them, were you in touch, and what course did these matters take?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-April, the northern area was deep in the war, first Derventa, then Odzak, Modrica and Samac. So Brod, Odzak and Derventa was placed under their control, and I mean the Croatian Muslim forces. There was fighting going around. Modrica and Samac, again, I think it was in mid-April, was placed under the control of the JNA. In all these areas, from that point on, it was the Crisis Staff that took charge of things and the centre no longer was in communication with any of the SJBs of the towns I mentioned. There was no communication in terms of information and in terms of traffic. In all those roads, barricades emerged. The municipality of Doboj was also divided. The villages such as Johovac, Kotorsko, Foca, and Komarica, that's the northern area facing the Sava river, was under the control of -- were under the control of the Croatian Muslim forces. The town proper, its urban core, was under the control of the joint JNA and police forces; whereas, the area beyond the town proper, namely, Carsija, Orasje and all the way up to Putnikovo Brdo, Alibegovci and then Civska, omega, et cetera, were under the control of the Muslim forces. Likewise, east of the Usora river, it's the place called Karuse, and the villages in the direction of Maglaj were also under their control. East of the tunnel on the main road leading to Tuzla, the villages of Stjepan Polje, Brijesnica, Klokotnica were under the control of the Muslim forces. Barricades were erected on these roads as well and the service was no longer able to function there. The village of Gradska was also under the control of -- well, there was a reserve police station there that had been mobilised and there were some other forces not belonging to the police, so these forces basically erected barricades, making it impossible to travel that way. Along all these roads, there were instances of car hijacking, plunder, the president of the Executive Board and president of the Municipal Assembly of Prnjavor were kidnapped. A JNA officer by the name of Ozegovic was also pulled over as he was travelling along the road and abducted. The stations of Maglaj and Tesanj, further to the south, were fully out of control of the CSB Doboj. The SJB Teslic, pursuant to a decision taken by the Municipal Assembly of Teslic, directed all of its work and the dispatches it sent out to the CSB Banja Luka. Therefore, the CSB in Doboj was left without its stations, and, as I told you, not even the entire Doboj area was under the control of either the CSB or its SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like in the SJBs Maglaj and Tesanj that belonged to you as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that they were fully out of control. They were -- there was no communication with them. The SCB [as interpreted] Doboj had no sort of control, no effective control under them -- over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, at that point in time, in late April, what sort of communication did the CSB have either the MUP of Republika Srpska or with the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there was a war on by that time, the communication was intermittent and finally ground to a complete halt. There was no communication whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think the last part of the answer was recorded. Did you say that there was no telephone or teleprinter communication?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, yesterday we talked about the MUP finances and specifically of the Security Services Centres. You said that the finances were left in the so-called joint MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, this situation, as it existed in April, as well as the disruption of communications, how did it reflect on the payment of salaries and all the other benefits due to the MUP members?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, salaries for the month of April were not paid out, nor were any funds intended for overhead expenses and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When did it happen for the first time that you received finances from the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska or, rather, from the government of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I recall, it was, at any rate, after the corridor was set up and after the collegium met in Belgrade. In other words, in July or was it early August? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will show you document 291D1; that's tab 38. It's a document which was written in July of 1992, as it seems, and it's a list of employees who have salaries due for April 1992. On page 2 of the document, there are signatures testifying to payments being made, receipts. And on page 3, a supplement to the list. Is there anything you can tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can see, this is a list of SJB members in Doboj. Where it says "Authorised official," I recognise the signature of Obrad Petrovic. And as for the two other signatures, I can't tell who they belong to. Likewise, on page 3, I do recognise the left-hand signature as that of Obrad Petrovic and the other two I don't recognise. And I can see that it has to do with the month of April. Yes, the list was made in July. It was probably a document based on which funds would be requested for the payment of salaries, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, in the course of April, May, June, and July, to the best of your knowledge, did members of the CSB or SJB receive any sort of reimbursement, such as salaries?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of May and June, none of it was paid out. And I'm sure about it, because I would have received my salary and I didn't. And I don't remember exactly what the situation was, whether it was in late July or early August that the salaries were finally paid out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the next document, which is behind tab 39, 190D1. Another list of sorts. It's a list of staff members. And on page 3, a list of staff members employed in the police club or hall, and apparently it relates to April of 1992. The preamble on page 1 reads: "CSB, the police centre or hall." It is a list of employs who, in the course of the month April 1992, performed the duties at this police station and received advance pay of salary for this month. Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you first off that there was no police social centre or hall in early April. Because what later came to serve as a police hall or centre was initially an old people's home, and at this point in time it was still an old people's home. What I suppose happened was that those employees who used to work in the old people's home also didn't have their salaries paid out, and this was a way of then paying the -- them the income due; or, in the alternative, this was a way to justify the disposal of some funds. There were stories circulating about funds having been taken from the SDK and perhaps those funds were syphoned off somewhere. But what I know for a fact is that there was no police social centre in existence in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that you said that it is possible that this document was drafted subsequently, in order to provide justification for the money that was taken from the vaults of the social auditing office, or seized in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that that could be one possible option.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, when was this money taken out from the social auditing office vault in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that took place in May.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there no objection, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Unless I'm missing something, Mr. Zecevic, I'm not sure -- what the witness says is that this doesn't -- his appreciation of this document is that it doesn't say what it purports on its face to say. Indeed, it's a cover for something else. So on what basis --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm withdrawing. I understand Your Honour's position. And I appreciate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, can you please look at -- but first of all, tell me, up until which date -- or actually, when was it that the conflict broke out in the town of Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened on the 2nd of May. I think on the night between -- or the period between the 1st and 3rd May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in Doboj on that date?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you just briefly describe the situation and what occurred.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said how the municipal territory was divided and what had happened with the northern and southern parts of the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, maybe, since you explained the region to us, maybe it would be beneficial for us to look at the map. That's tab 230, P1344. So maybe if you look at the map, you can better explain the situation to us and possibly make some markings, if necessary. With the assistance of the Court Officer, you would be handed a pen to make these markings.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which tab did you say it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 230. In front of you, you can see the map on the screen. Maybe it is more convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can just zoom in it for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is it enough?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is quite visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just tell us if you want to make any markings, and in that case we shall ask the Usher to give you a pen.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that the northern parts, up there, were under the control of the Croatian Muslim forces, and that some 17 villages in that area had already been ethnically cleansed. The Serbian population fled mainly towards Doboj and also to Banja Luka. So before this conflict in Doboj, the situation was being monitored and there were discussions in political circles and also with the JNA command, et cetera, and Cazim Hadzic, the garrison commander in Doboj, decided to pre-empt an attack from this part here that I mentioned earlier, coming from Carsija, Alibegovci, Susnjari, all the way to Alibegovo Brdo, because there was information indicating that the same scenario would be played out in Doboj as -- as in Derventa. That is why the commander decided to engage the army forces and to place the town under their control. That was carried out, if I remember correctly, between the 2nd and the 3rd of May. I know that there was an order issued to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Doboj garrison commander was Cazim Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic is a Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And he was the garrison commander of the JNA in Doboj, and, according to what you just said, if I understood you correctly, and correct me if I'm wrong, he was the one who ordered this operation to be carried out, in order to prevent an attack on Doboj. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. That was the order that he issued, in order to pre-empt an attack and the seizure of Doboj by paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us just briefly how this operation evolved and what happened and where the separation lines were.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the night between the 2nd and the 3rd, the commander's order was implemented. The forces entered the town - the JNA forces, I mean - and they took key positions in the urban quarters of the town. By that I mean certain intersections, institutions such as municipality building, the court building, the police building, the SDK building, banks, et cetera. In the morning, a request was sent out to the formations that were deployed above the town to surrender their weapons, and that would then prevent any fighting from taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What -- whose formations are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Muslims formations deployed above the town, and I believe that they were given a deadline by 1800 hours. I'm not quite sure, but I know it was definitely in the afternoon. I remember that before the deadline expired that the army had given them, an armed conflict broke out in which these paramilitary formations did not want to discuss any surrender of the weapons, but, rather, chose to advance towards the town, which resulted an armed conflict. According to what I know, that happened some time during the afternoon, because, at the time, I was in the police building. I think that it was quite late into the night when the fighting stopped and everything became calm, but the operations were -- continued the following day towards Putnikovo Brdo. As for the villages to the east of Doboj that I mentioned, such as Stjepan Polje, Brijesnica, Mala Klokotnica, and so on, remained under the control of Muslim forces and it was later declared Doboj istok or Doboj east municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If it is not problem for you, can we use the map in order to get a clear picture about the locations that you have been mentioning. Can you please mark where Doboj istok is, and if there are any other municipalities as well.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I made a mistake. I didn't realise it worked so fast. So here, to the right, this is Svjetlica Klokotnica and the border is up there. Stanic Rijeka, Brijesnica. Suho Polje was not included, so it would be approximately like this. Later on that became Doboj istok municipality. I'm not sure but I believe that included Lukavica as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please make a circle around what you think was Doboj istok.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it. Roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark it with the number 1. Put a number 1 in the middle of the circle.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you marked with the number 1 Doboj istok municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At that time was any other municipality formed; and, if so, can you show it to us on the map?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was Doboj jug, or Doboj south. I can't see very clearly and I'm having difficulties finding my bearings, but I think that it was here underneath -- it would have made it much easier for me if the river was there, but I see Matuzici, Karuse, et cetera, but that would be it. More or less due west of the river Bosna, like this. And then Usora municipality, which is west of Martinovac, Ularice, and I suppose you would ask me to mark this as well. Which number shall I put?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Put the number 2 and tell us what it indicates.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 2 indicates the municipality Doboj jug, and to the left is Usora municipality, comprising Martinovac, Ularice and this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please encircle it and put number 3.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's south of Prisade, so that would be Usora municipality. It is it not very accurate because this is a small scale and there are no topographic features, but that would be more or less the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, this means that the territory of Doboj municipality was divided, in fact, into four separate municipalities, i.e., number 1, Doboj jug; number 2 -- sorry number 1, Doboj istok; number 2, Doboj jug; and number 3, Usora municipality?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And as for the rest, we might say was the remaining part of the original Doboj municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have this photograph [as interpreted] tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D462, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you managed to save the markings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These municipalities still exist and function within the Federation. That's just what I would like to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Mr. Bjelosevic, you will have to put your markings again. It sometimes happens with this electronic equipment that we lose data. So, please mark with the circle and with the number 1 Doboj istok. You should better wait for the assistance ...

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we can enlarge it a bit as before, that would be good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Witness was asking if it can be enlarged a bit. I thought it was translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this okay?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes. I can do it now. I have trespassed into another municipality. You said number 1; is that right? I think that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have we managed to keep it this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Apparently the technological god is not with us, so the suggestion is that he use the paper copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, maybe I can return to that some other day, tomorrow or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. The -- while we have this brief interruption, I indicate that the staggered times I have worked out for today is that we would take the break at 11.50, resume at 12.10, and then rise for the day at 1.25, so counsel and the support staff should govern themselves accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, the municipalities that you marked and that we are going to mark yet again tomorrow, they're marked with numbers 1, 2 and 3. Doboj istok, jug and Usora. These are municipalities that came into being -- or actually, did they come into being then, around that point in time, the 3rd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, since then that is how it has been functioning. Everyone in his own area. They exist to this day under those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In these municipalities, what is the majority population?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doboj istok, Doboj jug, Bosnian population. And the municipality of Usora has a predominant Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the way these municipalities remained in accordance with the Dayton Agreement?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they're within the Federation on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, after these conflicts on the 2nd and 3rd of May, if I understood you well, what happened after that with the CSB Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already on the 3rd of May, when I came to the centre in the morning, I tried to convene a meeting of the top personnel that made up the collegium of the CSB. The communications were down. They were sort of on and off, but, at any rate, I didn't manage to convene the meeting. Then, during the course of the day, at a meeting in the Crisis Staff, we were asked to come to a meeting in the Crisis Staff, and the chief of the station was there as well, it was agreed that, since the centre no more had its territory, as you could see all of Doboj was not under the control of the CSB Doboj, and also due to the lack of personnel, as such, for it to be possible for departments to function, namely, the milicija, then the crime police and the administrative department and so on, it was decided that the public security station should function until further notice with its own elements, and that the personnel that remained and who were ethnic Serbs within the centre itself should be re-directed to the station so that the station could function in the best possible way. And that is, indeed, what was done. Therefore, since then, not a single department in the CSB hasn't functioned, except for the communications department. The centre for communications is a single one and it is used for the CSB and for the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A few questions. This collegium that you refer to, if I understood you correctly, you wanted to convene it on the 3rd of May, the collegium of the CSB. The members of that collegium, that is to say, the top personnel in the different departments within the CSB, were of which ethnic affiliations?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the Milicija department was Blagojevic, but the head of the sector for public security was Hasan Klokic. The head of the crime police was Pejo Krnic; he is a Croat. And I didn't say what the ethnic background of the other two was. Klokic is a Muslim, Blagojevic is a Serb. Pejo Krnic is a Croat. The head of the administrative and legal office was Mato Krizic, a Croat. The head of the fire department was Turolic. I cannot remember his first name but he was an ethnic Muslim. The head of the financial department was Dizdarevic. Right now, I don't seem to be able to remember his first name either. Yes, it is Mustafa, Mustafa Dizdarevic. He's a Muslim. And the head of the communications department was Jovan Spasic. He was a Serb. Ethnic Serbs responded to the invitation to attend this meeting. As to the others, none of them responded. None of them came. And what happened is what I referred to already, in terms of where different personnel went.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This decision that, in fact, the CSB, in fact, de facto, would stop operating and the public security station of Doboj would take over their powers and duties was actually a decision taken by which organ?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to explain this. It's not that they would take over the powers of the centre because the centre simply ceased to operate. The CSB Doboj simply ceased to operate. Because it had no territory. It would have been pointless for the centre to exist because it didn't have any stations under its control. And also, they did not have the personnel that was needed. So at that meeting of the Crisis Staff that was the decision that was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When this decision was made by the Crisis Staff, what happened with you then, as the chief of the centre that ceased to operate?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed the centre, as such, at that point in time, and I explained to them, and I actually made a suggestion to them and they went along with it, that, formally, we should not go into changing what was regulated by law, to say that that there would be no centre any longer. Rather, it was agreed that the service should function within the station. The centre would cease to operate until further notice, and I was directed towards the military because Operation Corridor was being prepared then. I would like to remind that you the area of the Krajina and this part, that is to say, part of the Doboj municipality, part of the Derventa municipality, that it was totally encircled. There was no way out of that territory at that point in time. That is when I became involved in that particular work. We prepared intelligence and other information. I was at the command post, at the forward command post of the 1st Krajina Corps on a more or less general basis. General Talic was there and his other assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since you are a member of the Ministry of the Interior, and you say that you were at the command post and you became involved in that, in what capacity did you become involved in this work with the military?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to make things clearer, allow me to give a more detailed explanation, if possible. In Yugoslavia, the concept system and doctrine were elaborated on the basis of the system of Total People's Defence and the system grew out of that. The Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, was the operative army that had its peacetime corps and its wartime units that were manned if there was an immediate threat of war. There were also certain structures that were area related. Those were the Territorial Defence units, the self-protection units, and the wartime police stations were among these structures too. In accordance with the Law on National Defence, the federal republican laws and the Law on the Armed Forces of the SFRY, the commander, a commander of a regiment, or a brigade, or bigger units than that, have the right to place under his command all area-related units within his area of responsibility and to command them. It is on that basis that I was involved in this planning and preparation of Operation Corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, at that point in time, in accordance with these regulations that you quoted a moment ago, you were resubordinated to the army, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry. One's hair always stands on end when you heard the words "if I understood you correctly," because it's -- counsel is just going to put what his own theory is. The word "resubordination" has not been mentioned. This is a matter at issue. There is to be no leading at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my mistake. I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, on the basis of what you said, when you say that, "On that basis I became involved," et cetera, which basis were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the regulations on the basis of which commanders were authorised to place all forces in the area of their responsibility under their command. On that basis, I became involved in preparing Operation Corridor, on the basis of the authorities stipulated by law, and also on the basis of a request from the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify this. Under whose command were you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, during the preparations, under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. Later on, I was appointed commander, and I became a part of Tactical Group 3. At the time, it was commanded by Colonel Lisica. He was a colonel then and later became a general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, just one moment. Mr. Bjelosevic, was this an order that concerned you individually? Were you placed under the command of the military as an individual, or was that order in regard to a corps or an institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the very beginning, it pertained to me personally so that I would become involved in the corps command. As for the complete forces of the milicija, immediately, practically from the 2nd or 3rd of May onwards, they were under the command of Operative Group Doboj. The Doboj Operative Group. I personally was engaged later within Tactical Group 3 that was commanded by Colonel Lisica. Of course, I was involved with a certain number of forces, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So I understand you well, the regulations on the basis of which commanders were authorised to place all forces in the area under their responsibility -- of their responsibility under their command, such an order could apply to an individual? That was within their competence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, the fact that you were placed under the command of the army, how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the 30th of June, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was it after that date and in the course of 1992, or even at a subsequent date, that you would again receive orders from the army command by which you were engaged in the army?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was called yet again to be engaged in the army as commander, pursuant to an order from the commander of the Operational Group Doboj, Mr. Lisica, because, once the initial task was accomplished, Tactical Group 3 was dissolved, and he was given the command over the Operational Group Doboj. Based on his order, it was sometime in November that I was appointed commander of a battalion and deployed to the Teslic front line, where I spent a certain period of time with the forces that were placed under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The forces that were placed under your command, were they members of the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a mixed composition. If I remember correctly, there were two, three, or four police structures. There was a military police company. And scouts, I believe. I also received forces that were to serve as my support, and I mean artillery support, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also the 5th Special Detachment of the special police forces. Yes. Those were the forces under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, all these members of the police, including yourself, during the time you spent in the army, in what capacity were you there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the duration of our engagement in the army, we formed a unified entity. We were fully subject to the regulations and the command of the army. Because what was at stake was the conduct of combat missions, and this was regulated under the Law on National Defence and the Law on Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bjelosevic, I'll show you a document, 1D259, which is behind tab 50. This is a Crisis Staff decision, 1D5 -- 259, tab 50.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a Crisis Staff decision dated the 15th of June, even though there is a reference in the text to a meeting held on the 15th of May. At the bottom, we see president of the Crisis Staff, a signature, and a stamp. Can you tell us, are you familiar with this decision? Did you attend the meeting? And what can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this decision. I was given a copy of it with the exact same contents. I wasn't there when it was made, but it does reflect the situation as it existed in early May, when the Crisis Staff charged the chief of the public security station to, within five days, see to it that all the decisions and conclusions by the Crisis Staff were implemented. Item 2 was related to me personally as the chief of centre. Under that item, I was asked to provide explanations for certain appointments, or, rather, ministry decisions that were received. Let me remind you that deputies attended a meeting of the Republika Srpska Assembly, or, rather, at the time it was the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They flew there by helicopter because the meeting took place at Pale. They brought along a number of documents, enactments issued by Minister Stanisic and gave them to me. This was roughly around the 15th of May, if I recall correctly. They gave me the documentation and asked that I provide explanations. It was a very difficult thing for me to do because we had had no communication whatsoever with the ministry of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In item 3, you can see that the station chief is charged with making lists of the senior staff and inspectors and sending them to the Crisis Staff, as the Crisis Staff was supposed to approve these lists. So we can already see that there's a hierarchy in place.
