And item 4 says that the Doboj municipality Crisis Staff orders all the groups and individuals present in the area of Doboj municipality, even there you can see that the municipality is not complete, who are charged with maintaining law and order to place themselves under the command of the chief of the SJB who is the only person authorised to organise and manage security-related issues in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we just clarify one thing. The head of the public security station was not you. Who was it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The head of the -- or the chief of the SJB Doboj was Obren Petrovic. Further, as part of this particular item, you can see that the chief was duty-bound to inform the Crisis Staff about the latest developments and the situation in Doboj, so the Crisis Staff made it incumbent on him to report back to them. And then the Crisis Staff expressed its support of the police, et cetera. Further down, the station chief is ordered to provide for an organised delivery of supplies to the police, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As you say, item 2 had to do with you. I seem to recall you saying that.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you act upon item 2?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the deputies came back from the minister with a set of documents and they wanted explanations for them. So I did. I provide them explanations for these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you look at 699D1, tab 52, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, if we're leaving that document, I know it's already an exhibit, can I just ask, is this a document provided by this witness to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which document are you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The Crisis Staff minutes that we have just been looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The decision by the Crisis Staff. It's the Exhibit 1D259.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. I just said that. I said I know it is already an exhibit. I'm merely querying, because it wasn't made clear at the time it was made an exhibit, whether this is a document provided [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will inform you after the break, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So 699D1, tab 52. This is a --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- conclusion, dated 22nd of June. The Serbian municipality of Doboj. It bears a signature, president of the Crisis Staff. Are you familiar with the document at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked to explain the regulations which applied to the ministry. Since I was engaged in the army, on a couple of occasions I was asked that, in keeping Minister Stanisic's instructions that CSB chiefs can at their own discretion assign their various members to different duties, I was asked that I should appoint myself a deputy -- appoint a deputy to my role. Milan Savic was nominated for the job, and he did not satisfy the requirements as provided, not for a deputy, because that did not exist, but for an assistant. I said that it wasn't a good solution because the candidate did not satisfy the requirements. They insisted on their choice. And that's why we have such a large interval, a long interval between the request that was put for me to explain these matters and the final conclusion adopting my explanations. After my resistance to the candidacy of Savic and explanations that this wasn't in accordance with the regulations, I was told that I should appoint him, that they would see to it and that once the contact with the ministry is re-established, they would be the ones to justify his appointment. Therefore, we agreed to do so, and I think it was on the 22nd or the 23rd of June that I appointed Milan Savic was assistant CSB Doboj, and I continued performing my duties within the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence, please: Conclusions of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Same question. I assume it comes from Mr. Bjelosevic as his name is on the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one second. We're checking. I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, did you provide us with this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I gave it to you or to the investigators. But this was my copy, and it was addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a document we received from the witness. I was just told by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D463, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One other short document which is 192D1, tab 53. Let's deal with it before the break. 192D1, tab 53.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a decision where I temporarily assigned Milan Savic to the post of assistant chief of the Security Services Centre in Doboj. We see the date, and the signature is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, it's a decision you issued.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this was a follow-up to what you were asked to do by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was done at the request of the Crisis Staff. Later on, the commander of the defence the town, Stankovic, asked me to do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D464, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I'm asking the same question. I was just going to remark it would really be much simpler, rather than me wasting time, getting up and asking each time, "Is this a document Bjelosevic gave," is if the Defence -- they don't have to, but it might save time, gave us a list of all the documents on their list which were supplied by this witness. Because, otherwise, I'm going to get up each time and ask the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We shall definitely provide that because we don't need these interruptions, pauses. I see the time, Your Honours. Can we take the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, if -- Your Honours, we have advised the Office of the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber, and -- the provenance of the documents. Let me just remind the Trial Chamber, that the document 1D259 was admitted through testimony of Prosecutor's Witness ST-162.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may be seated, sir. Yes, Mr. Zecevic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, just a short digression prompted by a response that you gave. I'd like to show you a document, 1D73, tab 46.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your response, you mentioned an order that you had received from the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, specifically from Minister Stanisic, relating to appointments. And just to paraphrase what you said, the Crisis Staff, based on that, asked to you make a specific appointment. Did that order refer -- or, rather, the instruction refer or does this document refer to this order and can you explain?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the decision by which Minister Stanisic is authorising heads of Security Services Centres and that was the decision that was brought to me by the deputies after the assembly session, and we discussed this issue on the Crisis Staff, and on this basis, they requested me to proceed with the appointment of Mr. Savic as assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the deputies brought this to you after the assembly session, I think that you mentioned in an earlier answer some helicopter flights. Is that related in any way?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because regular communication links were severed, and if the deputies wanted to attend the assembly meeting, they would go there, and on this occasion, they brought some documents with them and handed them over to me. I think that took place some time in mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did they fly by helicopter, these deputies?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only mode of transportation. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you another document, P1342, tab 233. Mr. Bjelosevic, this is a letter sent by -- at least that's what it says in the heading, Doboj Security Services Centre, dated the 17th of July, 1992. We have the typed name of Andrija Bjelosevic at the bottom. There is an stamp. But I think there is something handwritten in that part of the letter. Is that a letter of yours?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from the signature, there is an word "for" and it's another person's signature. I think this was signed by Milan Savic, and from the content of the document, you can see what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you authorise Mr. Savic to send out this letter; and was it sent with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not sent with my knowledge, and I didn't know anything about this document at the time. I only saw it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bjelosevic, can you just confirm for me whether it is true that, from the beginning of May until the 30th of June, you were discharging your duties in the military?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zecevic. Have you left this document that you had last put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, although you -- you said you had no knowledge of this until later, would it have been within the ordinary authority or practice of the CSB for whoever signed this document to have signed it on your behalf although would you not have been aware of it beforehand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure if I understood you correctly. But something like this shouldn't have left the centre at all and, truly, at the time when he drafted and signed this document, I knew nothing about it. And I wouldn't have agreed with it anyway. You saw that Savic came and became my assistant, contrary to my choice and contrary to my will, which resulted in poor communication between the two of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a partial answer to the question I have, but I still come back to notwithstanding the fact that you wouldn't have agreed with it, and notwithstanding the fact that you didn't know about it beforehand, whether, in the usual and ordinary arrangement, it is something that he could have done, could have properly done. "Properly" is probably the wrong word. That as a matter of routine that -- it's something that could have issued although you had no knowledge of it. That's my real question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, the assistant was entitled to sign certain documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more question relating to this, Mr. Bjelosevic. Was the police authorised to ask the investigating judge to release certain individuals?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that these kind of letters -- or let me ask you this: According to your knowledge, had any similar letter sent earlier from the Security Services Centre?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under the law, did you have this kind of authority at all? Could you make such a request to the investigating judge or the court?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those persons were under the jurisdiction of the court, and there was no basis whatsoever or any authority for anyone to write such a letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Up until which point, according to the Law on Criminal Procedure, can the police authority stretch during the so-called preliminary criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the filing of the criminal report and until the handing over of the suspects to the custody of the court. And the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After the filing of a criminal report and the handing over of a suspect, was police authorised to undertake any actions in relation to that case of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They could collect information relating to the case, provided they exist, and that they would pass this information to the investigating judge and the prosecutor's office. However, for the people in detention, they could not take any action whatsoever. Even if they wanted to interview them, they would have to ask approval from the judge to do that, and it was up to the judge to accept or to decline such a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was the police duty-bound at the request of investigating judge or a prosecutor to undertake certain actions as instructed by them?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in this instance - let me just remind you - that this was under the jurisdiction -- or, rather, the investigation was being conducted by a different centre, and there was no basis whatsoever for this kind of action or for this kind of letter to be written as Savic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about a specific case. I'm just talking about general powers that are in line with the Law on Criminal Procedure. According to the Law on Criminal Procedure or other regulations, did the police have any authority or any possibility to request anything from the investigating judge or the prosecutor, or to make any suggestions or issue instructions relating to their work?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was beyond their competence, and they didn't have this kind of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I move on, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, it would perhaps help if we could see the previous page of this document. Because I have no clue about what it is all about. We only saw -- saw the page with the signature. Unless I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry about that. I didn't see the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists, you didn't see the first page, but actually it is in connection with the arrest of the Mice. That is what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my document has only one page as far as I can see. Oh, I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I'm looking at the original and -- I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. But the problem is solved. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, let us go back to my question, if you can just give me a moment. It seems to me that you confirmed that you were in the military service from the 3rd of May until 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During that period, did you used to visit the Doboj CSB?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would come occasionally to my office there. The State Security Service was operating there at the time, and I would collect information from them that they gathered on the ground, and they provided useful intelligence about what we might encounter in the field and in the battlefield and in the general surrounding area, in terms of possible attacks that were being prepared from other directions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, from that period, do you know that there were any exchanges of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that something was happening in that domain, and I know that the Crisis Staffs established certain communications pertaining to exchanges of prisoners, but I was not personally involved in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, when you say "Crisis Staffs," do you mean Crisis Staffs from different sides of the front line, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I believe that goes without saying. It's not one and the same side that is going to exchange prisoners. It's going to be the two sides that are fighting each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Crisis Staffs existed on the other side as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that I've already said that, when I spoke about the situation in April. Already in -- at that point in time, Crisis Staffs had taken over in Brod, Samac, all these municipalities. Odzak, Derventa. Later on Modrica as well. Doboj, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at P1305, tab 46 -- 49. Before that, let me just ask you something, Mr. Bjelosevic. Did the police have any authority over the prison or prisons? I mean, according to the law, and according to the rules and regulations of the service and the Law on the Interior and specifically the CSB of Doboj, did it have any authority in relation to the central prison in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The prisons had their own security services, and police authority did not extend to these institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which ministry or which part of the state administration the prisons belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Justice had prisons within their province of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the case with the central prison in Doboj, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at P1305, tab 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, this is a document dated the 12th of June, 1992. It is an order. At the bottom of the page, what is typewritten is "Head of the centre, Andrija Bjelosevic," and there is a seal and a signature. Tell me, is this your document? Are you familiar with this document and what can you tell us about the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that I signed and that I dictated so that it would be typed up, and it was done in quite a bit of a hurry as I was coming to the centre. It was either the prison warden or his deputy that I came across, and this person told me that they had certain problems regarding the entry of different persons wearing different uniforms, that they would violently enter the premises of the prison, and that they committed violent acts against the prisoners there. And this person asked for help. When I entered the building, I think that I came across Mladen Vulic, and I dictated this to him. I did it off the cuff. Perhaps the wording is not the best possible but it does reflect the situation as it was. When it was typed up, I signed it. I said that this should be put on the bulletin board in the police building, and I said that it should be provided to the station as well. Also, that he should tell Chief Petrovic that the police should help the service running the prison, because they were nearby, if they could help them so that this kind of thing would not happen again. Whenever I see this, I remember a situation that happened to me personally after this order, when I came to the centre once again, when people with rifles were waiting for me there, four of them. One of them was Petar Petrusic. He was a very violent man. And later on, he killed Luka Radojcic, a lieutenant-colonel who was commander of Tactical Group Ozren, and his commander. He killed him using a fire-arm. It was shocking when I entered the premises and when I experienced that. I asked what this was all about. He pointed a pump action rifle at my head. He cocked the rifle, and they said that I was a Serb Ustasha and that I was protecting Ustashas and Balijas. I looked at the bulletin board, because it was in the hallway there, and I saw this order. I saw that they used cellotape to put it up there, and it was stabbed with a knife. I brought the original here now, with the cellotape and with those traces, so if you wish -- if you want me to, I can show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, you handed this document over to the investigators of the OTP, or, rather, was that the case?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When they interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was in 2004 in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness volunteered he has an original document if the Trial Chamber would like to see it. I'm at your hands -- in your hands entirely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... he -- can I confirm, as Your Honours can see at the top of the page, that's why it's one of the documents that I was discussing this morning. You will see it says "AB 13" and it's signed. He handed over in the document, that's when the writing was put on. But I'm sorry, when did he volunteer to produce the original? Oh, I see the one that he's just --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. I missed that bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's not original but it's the copy that was with the cellotape with the knife mark through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's the only original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. No, I'm not taking issue with that it's the original, but for what purpose do you think that this document would be useful? We know what the content of the document was. Whether we're dealing with one of a number of copies of the original is neither here nor there for these purposes. But he has described this particular incident and I'm not sure how the -- how it assists that, beyond what he has already said. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, can I ask so that we don't have to go back to this. Is the witness saying that what he gave to us in interview is a copy of another copy or a copy of the original with, as he asserts, the knife thrusts through it. That's what I'm not clear about at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe, Your Honours, the answer is -- is obvious. Why is it needed that the witness shows the original? According to Ms. Korner's question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, all I simply want to know is he saying that he has two copies of this. One which he provided a copy of us to, or -- and another one which he has -- alleges has this knife thrust?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And my question is: Does it matter? He --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may do. It may do, Your Honour. [Microphone not activated] ... that part of the question, whether he says he has two entirely separate copies, may -- may matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As Ms. Korner has said, something may turn on this. So let's proceed. Carefully, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, if you can, would you please show us this document and then explain to us whether that document is the original and what you see in front of you, in the binder and on the monitor, whether that is the copy of that document or some other document.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the copy that was on the bulletin board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you hand it to the Usher first. The Usher will then show it to counsel on both sides and then Mr. Zecevic will ask you to speak to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, you will see it is clear they are two entirely separate copies. Unless the holes were put in afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- what we see has an original stamp on it. So it appears to an original. It may be a copy -- well, copy. Well, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, if Your Honours look at what's on the screen, there is nothing to indicate from the photocopy that we took certainly -- I say "we," that the OTP took back in 2004 to show that any of such markings on it. So the question is: Where does this copy come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can put it on the ELMO. If it's needed, Your Honours. Or I can just ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, this document that you have there in the original now, in that plastic cover, is that the document that you placed on the bulletin board on the CSB in Doboj in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the document that you saw the second time when you returned, when this incident occurred involving these four men, is that the document that you saw in the very same bulletin board, stabbed with knife?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with these holes that you can see now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do with the document after that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left it there. This was photocopied and it is the photocopy of this document that I handed over to the investigators in 2004. If you focus on some details, will you see that that is the situation. First of all, in the preamble where it says, "On the basis of the Law on Interior," et cetera, you will see, that where the hole is, you cannot see the letter N and you cannot see the letter A. Also, you will see -- in the upper part of page, you will see traces of cellotape on the copy, to the left of where my signature was placed when I handed over the document, the AB number, et cetera. And you will see in the right-hand corner, at the bottom, you will see traces of cellotape underneath my signature there. If you focus on all of this, you will see that this is precisely the document that was photocopied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you want me to pursue this anymore? Is there any need? Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, thank you very much. That's very helpful. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, I'm going to show you another document, 193D1, tab 54. The date of the document is the 27th of June, 1992. It was sent to public security stations, and the signature is that of the centre -- the chief of the centre, Andrija Bjelosevic. There is a signature there. I don't know whether you can see it properly.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature. And this is the content of a document that I wrote. It has to do with certain problems that had been noted. The objective of this order of mine was to oppose that, to have the police, the milicija, prevent this kind of behaviour on the part of groups and individuals, to gather information about persons and locations, namely, individuals who had committed unlawful acts, and locations where they left the property that they had stolen so that that could be found later. As for the procedure with property that was seized by the police at check-points, that should be left at check-point -- at collection points and that proper certificates should be provided on the seizure of such goods. Also, policemen should energetically oppose wilful behaviour on the part of groups an individuals, in terms of entering apartments belonging to other people, arresting persons, et cetera. If such operative work is necessary, then legal procedure should be followed. Because I was receiving information to the effect that there was unlawful action taken by persons who had introduced themselves as belonging to the police. Since this was already the end of June, the corridor was established already on the following day, and it was quite obvious that certain territories were being liberated and stations would be established there, so I gave people this task, and I said that these stations should receive copies of this same document. The Petrovo station had already started functioned by then. Modrica had already been liberated. Derventa Grad was about to be liberated in a matter of days, and that's why I addressed it to all of them. As for this part of the municipality of Maglaj, in Jablanica, a public security station had already started operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw the two documents from June, in one and the previous one. During your stay in the army, would you, from time to time, go to the CSB Doboj to perform certain duties?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would go there on occasion, though, admittedly, I would not stay there for long periods of time. I told you already that my visits there primarily had to do with certain information relevant to the conduct of the corridor operation. In other words, intelligence. On those occasions, I would always meet up with some of the people in the service who would brief me on issues as briefly as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You've already referred to -- in some of the documents to the -- or, rather, when discussing that document, you said that you were exposed to threats and unpleasant situations. Did it happen again? Were you again exposed to such a situation within the centre; and, if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would happen frequently that certain formations which had in early May wrested themselves out of the control of the MUP -- let me digress briefly. When -- I think it was in early April that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was declared. By that time, the area was rife clashes. Certain combat groups and units that were part of the JNA would leave the -- their superior units would wrest themselves out of their control and act independently and arbitrarily. On several occasions, they engaged in hostile behaviour toward the police force and police stations, including myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, on such occasions, when you were threatened, were these threats serious? Were they a cause for concern to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it's serious when someone points a rifle to your head and cocks it. Then the threat cannot be more serious than it is. You're just waiting to hear the trigger being pulled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I move to something else, I was reminded that I didn't offer this document for admittance. So it's Defence 65 ter 193D1, tab 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D465, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, please have a look at another document bearing your signature, which is 65 ter 194D1, tab 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, I'd like to check something first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 194D1, tab 55.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a work-plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment, please. Let me put my question first. The date on this document is also the 27th of June, 1992. There is a typed signature, chief of centre. The signature is not particularly visible. And it was sent to some of the public stations, public security stations. Can you tell us, is this your document, and what is the reason why it was made?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Modrica municipality, there was a paramilitary group present, and the members it comprised are listed in this document. This was not in Modrica proper. It was to the south, the villages of Koprivna and Vranje. While Operation Corridor was still going on, information was received about this group being violent, engaging in plunder, stealing vehicles from the police force, and they were characterised as very violent and dangerous. Since this was a paramilitary formation, we agreed that they would be arrested. We, in the army. And they were arrested quite in advance of the date stated here, and together with the documents that were found on them, they were forwarded to the military prosecutor's office in Banja Luka. They were transferred there. They were placed in detention there, on remand, and after a while, the group was released. When they were taken to the military remand facility in Banja Luka, one Nikodin Cavic, who used to be a priest apparently, came to Doboj with four more men. People saw them step into the police building. This man was looking for me. He told them my name, and I was told that they had Skorpion weapons with silencers fitted on them. Apparently he broke open into my office to check whether I was, indeed, away, because he was told that I wasn't there. He stormed into my office, saw that I wasn't there, and then they left. Later on, when this group of people was released -- and, as you see, the document says according to the available information, there is a possibility for the group to reappear in the area, hence my order. Aware of how dangerous they were, I specified in my order that should they put up any resistance, they should be restrained by all means. There was a possibility that they might place the lives of policemen at risk, and that's why I said that they should use all means available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One question. Did you have any information to the effect that this same group had in the earlier period or -- or had been prone to committing crimes against members of other ethnicities? In other words, war crimes.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That they broke into their homes, plundering. The properties involved were in the direction of Modrica. There were Muslims there. The village was called Tarevci [phoen]. And, in some cases, the victims were Croats as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you know whether the 14 individuals listed here were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know them personally, but it transpired later on, from various documents, that they hailed from different areas, as you can see here, from Belgrade, Nis ... in other words, a heterogeneous group in terms of their backgrounds. There's Negotin there as well. They formed a group that was quite problematic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that His Honour Judge Delvoie has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, you said, on the one hand, "we, the military, arrested or decided to arrest them." And this document is a document signed, "I, the chief of CSB," right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's a little bit confusing for me, so if you could clarify the different caps you were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best. I will try to explain this. They were arrested before this date, the date of this order. Some 15 days earlier perhaps, and they were arrested by the military police with the assistance of, I believe, policemen from Modrica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I understood that, Mr. Bjelosevic. But on the date of this document, the 27th of June, you are still in the military, as you have told us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the information we got was that the group would re-emerge. First of all, in the area of the municipality of Modrica where a station was in the making. And I already told you where it was that we had functioning stations. Now, since the army released them - and I don't know why this was done - in my view, it was now up to the police to arrest them, because they were released from remand with military authorities, and I considered them to be a dangerous group. That's why this order was sent to public security stations. It became obvious that the corridor operation would soon be brought to an end. On the 28th, the corridor was broken open. I was preparing to go back to the centre and to restore the system of functioning SJB. I was already contemplating the idea to set up the various departments that were supposed to operate under the law within the Security Services Centre in Doboj, and I was trying to deal with the events just before they would actually happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So you were acting as chief of a CSB while being in the military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first steps to set up the centre were only to be made. We still didn't have a crime service, a legal service. I was trying to anticipate the events. The centre was yet to be given its various elements, but I was trying, nevertheless, to act as a centre chief. Because formally there was a document appointing me to that position, even though I was in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what was your function then in the army? What were you actually doing in the army? I mean, at that precise moment, in June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, it already had to do with the intelligence department, so I was dealing with intelligence, the analysis of intelligence as to what was going on in the enemy ranks, the enemy just opposite us and around us. My duty as commander -- perhaps that's what you're interested in. My duty as commander ceased when a line was reached in the direction of Derventa; we don't have a map here. It's a topographic feature, the Karaula or the border crossing. So the positions were reached. I remained within the command of the 1st Krajina Corps at a forward command post which was in Duge Njive, south of Modrica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So basically you had two different jobs at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One could put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's one other matter, if I may. Mr. Zecevic asked the witness, at page 68, line 22: "Can you tell us if you know whether the 14 individuals listed here were Serbs?" I think he meant of Serb ethnicity. I don't think that question was asked -- answered, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please answer the question repeated by Ms. Korner? And I'm grateful to her for reminding me of that question.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were member of the Serbian community, or the Serb ethnicity, and you can see that by their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, before I put my next question --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, lest there is no -- or -- unless there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D466, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, for how long did you command the unit on the battle-field during the corridor operation? Can you give me a date?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think that was up until the 22nd, 23rd, or 24th of June. But after that date, I'm sure that it was disbanded and the regrouping of the military forces took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So after the disbanding and regrouping of members of that unit, if I understood you correctly, you were transferred to the command, more specifically to the forward command post of the 1st Krajina Corps in Duge Poljane. Now what were your duties in the command?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the location is Duge Njive, not Duge Poljane. As I said, I was in the intelligence department of the command, and my duty was to collect and analyse intelligence relating to the enemy army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this intelligence department was attached to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And I was a sort of intermediary between the State Security Service and the command, and then together with them, we would assess the information or cross-reference information and then, later on, this information would be used by the commanders on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if you now, this: During the time you were in the military unit -- let me just phrase the question precisely. I think that we already saw a document, and if you can remind me, when was it that this person, Savic, was appointed your assistant at the CSB?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that practically between the 3rd of May and the 23rd of June, there was no executive staff in the Doboj CSB?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. There were no departments and there were no executive staff in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This man, Savic, did he have an executive position, and did he discharge these duties accordingly at the centre until you returned to the centre on or around the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He acted individually, so to speak, because, I would like to reiterate once again, the centre didn't have its essential parts. There were no departments, so he acted individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. Perhaps this is a good point that I can -- or maybe I have just one more document which is connected with the previous one so we can use up the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah, I was going to ask if you couldn't make use of the ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please look at 197D1, tab number 60. This is a document entitled "Work-plan," compiled on the 7th of July, 1992, and on page 2, we will see in the left-hand corner that it says that the plan was approved by Andrija Bjelosevic and who drew up this plan and who also agreed with it. Can you explain to us briefly what this is all about, and is it connected to the previous document?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a connection. In the meantime, between that order and this date, I don't know exactly when this group was re-arrested, because I was in hospital in Doboj at the time, but people from the service came to visit me and we discussed this topic, among other things. This plan was endorsed by Vojo Blagojevic and he signed it, and it was drawn up Inspectors Jovan Gostic and Veljko Solaja. These inspectors were working at the centre until early May, and as the territory became liberated, I was counting on them, that once we start establishing the centre -- and I wanted them to be given to me to form the criminal investigation department at the centre. Blagojevic accepted to become the head of this department for criminal investigation. When this group was arrested, a problem arose about what to do with them. The prosecutor's office and the investigating judge did not want to take in those individuals or any reports against them, due to lack of evidence. Everything that accompanied them at the time when they were first arrested, all the evidence, was sent alongside them in the files that were taken away by the military police. Now, we were facing people under arrest but we did not have any evidence about the crimes that they were suspected of having committed. Now, we drew up this plan in an attempt to carry out these activities as envisaged in the plan, with a view to acquiring elements that would be sufficient for these individuals to be processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If there's no -- [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, if there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D467, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I remember correctly, you have instructed us to complete by 1.20, and with that in mind, I would like to finalise my examination for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It was actually 1.25, but if you can't make use of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to, in any event, raise a question of future timing, so that we could do it now, rather than Mr. Zecevic going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bjelosevic, we are about to take the adjournment for the day. We will resume tomorrow morning. We will be in a different courtroom tomorrow morning, but you will be escorted there. So you will be escorted from the courtroom now. We are going to rise shortly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this morning we were informed that, so far, because of the various discussions and legal aspects, Mr. Zecevic had only used up something like, in two days, five hours of his allotted 20 hours. I don't know how much he has done today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Seven hours, I've been advised.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, in those circumstances, the examination-in-chief is not going to finish until Tuesday or Wednesday of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will definitely try my best to shorten the time of the direct examination but it might be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, I understand, but I can't stand on my feet more than seven days. So ... no, I think -- I think I would -- I would be able to finish perhaps, perhaps by Monday or early Tuesday, my direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is then Mr. Krgovic to go, and though I appreciate he isn't going to be very long, Your Honours, there is no way that can I complete my cross-examination by the end of Thursday. That would give me approximately six hours or something like that. So, Your Honours, in those circumstances, I would not wish to start cross. I do not want there to be a gap of ten days between the beginning of my cross-examination and the continuation. Your Honours, that's the application I make. There are such obvious reasons for this that I hope I needn't spell them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will think about this overnight, of course; but perhaps when we return tomorrow morning, counsel, plural, could indicate in that scenario what best use would be made of the two days. But we would speak to this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we take the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
